qti-assessment-test.title: PDHengineer - Structural Gusset-Plate Ethics & 2020 NEC Article 210/230 Self-Study PDH (Demo)

qti-assessment-item.title: Apply NSPE Code of Ethics Section II.1 and state P.E. sealing rules to unverified gusset-plate dead-load increases modeled on the I-35W collapse.

qti-item-body.p: Objective: Apply NSPE Code of Ethics Section II.1 and state P.E. sealing rules to unverified gusset-plate dead-load increases modeled on the I-35W collapse.

qti-choice-interaction.qti-prompt: A licensed P.E. retained to review a steel deck-truss bridge deck rehabilitation discovers that adding a 2-inch polymer concrete overlay pushes Node U10 gusset-plate demand-to-capacity ratios to 1.18 because original connection sheets were omitted from prior load ratings. The agency project manager instructs the P.E. to seal the overlay bid package today to preserve federal grant funding and defer gusset-plate retrofits to a future contract. Under NSPE Code of Ethics Section II.1 and NCEES Model Rules, what must the P.E. do?
qti-choice-interaction.qti-simple-choice: Seal the overlay plans with a cover-letter disclaimer shifting gusset-plate liability to the agency's maintenance division.
Refuse to seal the noncompliant overlay plans, advise the client of the structural overstress consequences, and notify the proper authority if overruled.
Approve the plans conditionally provided construction equipment staging loads are verbally restricted by the prime contractor.
Withdraw from the contract without notice while keeping the Node U10 overstress calculation confidential under client confidentiality rules.

qti-content-body.p: Incorrect. Contractual disclaimers do not cure sealing plans that violate governing AASHTO structural safety standards under NCEES Model Rules.
Correct. NSPE Code of Ethics Section II.1.a-b prohibits approving non-conforming plans that endanger public safety and mandates notifying proper authorities when safety judgment is overruled.
Incorrect. Even without staging loads, a permanent dead-load demand-to-capacity ratio of 1.18 exceeds allowable structural limits and cannot be sealed.
Incorrect. Under NSPE Section II.1.c, client confidentiality yields to the paramount duty to disclose imminent structural hazards to proper authorities.

qti-assessment-item.title: Apply 2020 NEC Article 210.8(A) voltage-range revisions to 240V dwelling laundry receptacles.

qti-item-body.p: Objective: Apply 2020 NEC Article 210.8(A) voltage-range revisions to 240V dwelling laundry receptacles.

qti-choice-interaction.qti-prompt: An electrical P.E. is designing branch circuits under the unamended 2020 NEC (NFPA 70) for a new single-family residence. The laundry room includes a dedicated 120/240V, 30-ampere, 4-wire receptacle feeding an electric clothes dryer located 8 feet horizontally from the edge of the laundry utility sink. Which protection rule governs this 240V receptacle?
qti-choice-interaction.qti-simple-choice: No GFCI protection is required because the receptacle is rated 240V rather than 125V.
GFCI protection is omitted because the receptacle sits more than 6 feet from the inside edge of the laundry sink.
Class A GFCI protection is required because 2020 NEC 210.8(A)(10) covers all 125V through 250V receptacles installed in dwelling laundry areas.
Combination AFCI protection alone satisfies 210.8(A)(10) for 30-ampere 240V appliance circuits.

qti-content-body.p: Incorrect. The 2020 NEC revised 210.8(A) to cover all single-phase receptacles rated 125V through 250V (150V or less to ground), eliminating the 125V exemption.
Incorrect. While 210.8(A)(7) uses a 6-foot sink measurement for non-kitchen/non-laundry sinks, 210.8(A)(10) covers the entire dwelling laundry area regardless of sink distance.

Correct. Under 2020 NEC 210.8(A) and 210.8(A)(10), a 120/240V (120V to ground) dryer receptacle in a dwelling laundry area requires Class A GFCI protection (typically via a 2-pole GFCI circuit breaker).
Incorrect. AFCI protection (210.12) applies to 120V, 15A and 20A circuits and never substitutes for shock-preventing Class A GFCI protection.

qti-assessment-item.title: Verify 2020 NEC 230.67 surge-protective device and 230.85 exterior emergency disconnect requirements on dwelling service replacements.

qti-item-body.p: Objective: Verify 2020 NEC 230.67 surge-protective device and 230.85 exterior emergency disconnect requirements on dwelling service replacements.

qti-choice-interaction.qti-prompt: When replacing a dwelling unit's 100A service panelboard with a new 200A service under the unamended 2020 NEC, the engineer specifies an outdoor meter-main feeding an indoor subpanel. Which combination satisfies both 2020 NEC 230.67 and 230.85?
qti-choice-interaction.qti-simple-choice: Install a listed Type 1 or Type 2 Surge-Protective Device integral to or immediately adjacent to the service equipment, and mark the readily accessible outdoor meter-main 'EMERGENCY DISCONNECT, SERVICE DISCONNECT'.
Install a Type 3 point-of-use surge strip at the kitchen receptacle circuit and place the sole service disconnect inside the locked basement.
Omit the SPD because 230.67 applies only to new construction, while installing an unmarked outdoor meter socket.
Label the outdoor meter-main 'FIRE PUMP DISCONNECT' and install a Type 4 component assembly without listing.

qti-content-body.p: Correct. 2020 NEC 230.67(A)-(D) requires a Type 1 or Type 2 SPD on dwelling service replacements, and 230.85(1) permits the outdoor service disconnect to serve as the emergency disconnect when marked 'EMERGENCY DISCONNECT, SERVICE DISCONNECT'.
Incorrect. 230.67(B) explicitly restricts service surge protection to Type 1 or Type 2 SPDs, and 230.85 mandates a readily accessible outdoor emergency disconnect.
Incorrect. 230.67(D) explicitly triggers Type 1 or Type 2 SPD installation whenever existing dwelling service equipment is replaced.
Incorrect. 230.85 mandates exact standardized emergency disconnect text, and Type 4 assemblies are not permitted as field-installed dwelling service SPDs under 230.67(B).
